newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FEATURE - Change means worst of both worlds for Russia miners.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Change means worst of both worlds for Russia miners.

text.p: The signposts on the new snowlined highway between the Siberian towns of Kemerovo and Novokuznetsk are blue, not red, but the slogans on them have a distinctly communist ring.
"This road is 30 percent less stressful on the driver," boasts one sign. "An end to impassable roads in the Kuzbass!" declares another.

Taxi driver Sergei Lykov remembers when travellers got trapped in bitter Siberian snowstorms and died of exposure. He said his father used to drive with bottles of vodka to swap for a tractor tow through streams where there were no bridges.
But while Lykov is glad of the road -- just lightly dusted with snow -- he can see why many locals are not. "New roads are one thing, going without your pay is quite another," he said.

The highway plan is not the only high-profile project which has raised hackles among the hundreds of thousands of have-nots in the Kuzbass -- a bleak, windswept coal mining region sunk in a mire of post-communist debts.

The regional centre Kemerovo has a new, but as yet unused "international" airport and richly-decorated churches have been put up among the mining and metallurgical plants which churn out sulphurous smoke.
The new facilities would be a source of pride to the region's inhabitants, if they could only get someone to do something about their plight.
PLIGHT OF THE KUZBASS
Driven to despair by the struggle to survive on home-grown vegetables and contributions from luckier relatives, the people of the Kuzbass have gone to dramatic lengths to appeal for help.
Pensioners have lain down on the road to stop traffic, mine rescue workers have gone on hunger strike and miners have staged sit-ins underground.

One man, caught in a struggle with his boss, tried to blow himself up in the centre of town. Another threw a grenade inside a bank he was trying to rob. He injured 14 people and got away with just 10,000 roubles, less than two U.S. dollars.

In November 100,000 miners went on strike for several days, threatening coal stocks which are crucial for heating in the freezing Siberian region. They won promises of help from the government, but are pessimistic about seeing the cash.
MINERS SAY THEY PAVED THEIR WAY TO HELL

Two things gall the miners most. The first is that, by taking part in mass protests in 1989, they helped bring in the changes which have left them penniless. Secondly, whatever they may do now, they are unable to turn back the clock.
"No one thought that the country would be destroyed, that enterprises would be brought to their knees," said Oleg Kuslitsy, a miner who has not been paid for six months.
"No one thought that we were paving the way to hell."
The governor of the Kuzbass, Mikhail Kislyuk, rose to power in the Kuzbass through the 1989 strikes and protests which helped Boris Yeltsin oust Mikhail Gorbachev from the Kremlin.
After he became president in 1991, Yeltsin rewarded Kislyuk for helping lead the Kuzbass strikes by appointing him governor.
Since then developments in the Kuzbass have turned out to be a microcosm of those in Russia as a whole.
Markets have opened up, bringing Western executives to the bleak Siberian steppes to fill the shops with their goods.

The World Bank has lent money to help reorganise the coal industry, where most of the pits are lossmaking. Local authorities have issued promissory notes to ease a cash crisis and signed a big agro-industrial contract with an Italian firm.
PIRANHAS SWIM IN MURKY SIBERIAN WATERS
But all this reform has only benefited a few in the Kuzbass, and then, by the authorities' admission, not always through honest means.

"They used the miners to destroy the Soviet Union so they could buy Mercedes cars and villas," said Vladislav, folding up the Soviet flag he had waved in vain at the regional administration building during the recent strike.

An airport worker demonstrating in solidarity with the miners, Vladislav was vague about who he had in mind, but even the struggling Kuzbass has its fair share of huge, new brick houses and luxury cars with tinted windows to hide their owners.
And piranhas, according to local newspapers, whose reports hinted the pet owners were as bad as their pets.

"Man-eating piranhas have replaced mini-crocodiles and pythons as the latest craze among Kemerovo's "New Russians'," said the Kuznetski Krai daily, using the derisive term for those deemed to have made large sums of money through crime.
Five piranhas cost 250,000 roubles ($50), excluding the aquarium and food, said the paper. "And by the way, how much is human flesh?" it concluded.

Deputy Governor Anatoly Pronin agrees that many people have got rich by stealing. "There was no legal way to become rich here," he said, adding by way of justification that the roots of American capitalism had been just as violent and wild.
"They're always accusing us of slavery, ill-placed spending and so on...What can I say to that? That 16 commissions checked us out and they didn't take anyone to court."
There was only one exception, he said, but in that case the accused was granted an amnesty.
With the local administration blaming the government for the cash squeeze and the government blaming the local administration for not collecting tax, the workers do not know where to turn.
Yuri Popov, head of the mining union in Prokopievsk, said miners should sue their bosses, but they are afraid of losing out on future pay or the goods they are sometimes given instead.
The strike, he said, was just a game. "Our leaders are used to sitting around the same table with the authorities and they do not know how to bang their fists on it."
Miner Viktor Trofinov says he was sorry he played a role in bringing Yeltsin to power. He did not want a return to communism, he added, "but we haven't seen democracy".
Kislyuk, like some of his communist predecessors, is taking a long view, although he invokes God rather than Marx.

"It's God's will, to toil and leave," he told the Izvestia newspaper, brushing off the workers' criticisms. "Then they can swear at me as much as they like, but I will go and the roads and churches that I have built will remain."
